source_text: Θυσία δὲ ἡ τῷ θεῷ δεκτὴ σώματός τε καὶ τῶν τούτου παθῶν ἀμετανόητος χωρισμός. ἡ ἀληθὴς τῷ ὄντι θεοσέβεια αὕτη. καὶ μή τι εἰκότως μελέτη θανάτου διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται τῷ Σωκράτει ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὁ γὰρ μήτε τὴν ὄψιν παρατιθέμενος ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι μήτε τινὰ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων ἐφελκόμενος, ἀλλ’ αὐτῷ καθαρῷ τῷ νῷ τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐντυγχάνων τὴν ἀληθῆ φιλοσοφίαν μέτεισιν. τοῦτο ἄρα βούλεται καὶ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ ἡ τῆς πενταετίας σιωπή, ἣν τοῖς γνωρίμοις παρεγγυᾷ, ὡς δὴ ἀποστραφέντες τῶν αἰσθητῶν ψιλῷ τῷ νῷ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύοιεν. παρὰ Μωυσέως τοιαῦτα φιλοσοφήσαντες οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἄκροι. προστάσσει γὰρ τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα δείραντας εἰς μέλη διανεῖμαι, ἐπειδὴ γυμνὴν τῆς ὑλικῆς δορᾶς γενομένην τὴν γνωστικὴν ψυχὴν ἄνευ τῆς σωματικῆς φλυαρίας καὶ τῶν παθῶν πάντων, ὅσα περιποιοῦσιν αἱ κεναὶ καὶ ψευδεῖς ὑπολήψεις, ἀποδυσαμένην τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας, τῷ φωτὶ καθιερωθῆναι ἀνάγκη. οἱ δὲ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ θνητὸν ἐνδυόμενοι καθάπερ οἱ κοχλίαι καὶ περὶ τὰς αὑτῶν ἀκρασίας ὥσπερ οἱ ἐχῖνοι σφαιρηδὸν εἱλούμενοι περὶ τοῦ μακαρίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου θεοῦ τοιαῦτα οἷα καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν δοξάζουσιν. λέληθεν δ’ αὐτούς, κἂν πλησίον ἡμῶν τύχωσιν, ὡς μυρία ὅσα δεδώρηται ἡμῖν ὁ θεός, ὧν αὐτὸς ἀμέτοχος, γένεσιν μὲν ἀγένητος ὤν, τροφὴν δὲ ἀνενδεὴς ὤν, καὶ αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν, εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως ὑπάρχων. διὸ καὶ χεῖρας καὶ πόδας καὶ στόμα καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ εἰσόδους καὶ ἐξόδους καὶ ὀργὰς καὶ ἀπειλὰς μὴ πάθη θεοῦ τις ὑπολάβῃ παρὰ Ἑβραίοις λέγεσθαι, μηδαμῶς, ἀλληγορεῖσθαι δέ τινα ἐκ τούτων τῶν ὀνομάτων ὁσιώτερον, ἃ δὴ καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου κατὰ τὸν οἰκεῖον καιρὸν διασαφήσομεν. ἦ πανακὲς πάντων φάρμακον ἁ σοφία, Καλλίμαχος ἐν τοῖς ἐπιγράμμασι γράφει· ἕτερος (δὲ) ἐξ ἑτέρου σοφὸς τό τε πάλαι τό τε νῦν, φησὶ Βακχυλίδης ἐν τοῖς Παιᾶσιν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ῥᾷστον ἀρρήτων ἐπέων πύλας ἐξευρεῖν· καλῶς ἄρα Ἰσοκράτης ἐν τῷ Παναθηναϊκῷ τίνας οὖν καλῶ πεπαιδευμένους; προθεὶς ἐπιφέρει· πρῶτον μὲν τοὺς καλῶς χρωμένους τοῖς πράγμασι τοῖς κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἑκάστην προσπίπτουσι καὶ τὴν δόξαν ἐπιτυχῆ τῶν καιρῶν ἔχοντας καὶ δυναμένην ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ στοχάζεσθαι τοῦ συμφέροντος· ἔπειτα τοὺς πρεπόντως καὶ δικαίως ὁμιλοῦντας ἀεὶ τοῖς πλησιάζουσι καὶ τὰς μὲν τῶν ἄλλων ἀηδίας καὶ βαρύτητας εὐκόλως καὶ ῥᾳδίως φέροντας, σφᾶς δ’ αὐτοὺς ὡς δυνατὸν ἐλαφροτάτους καὶ μετριωτάτους τοῖς ξυνοῦσι παρέχοντας· ἔτι δὲ τοὺς τῶν μὲν ἡδονῶν κρατοῦντας, τῶν δὲ συμφορῶν μὴ λίαν ἡττωμένους, ἀλλ’ ἀνδρωδῶς ἐν αὐταῖς ἀναστρεφομένους καὶ τῆς φύσεως ἀξίως ἧς μετέχοντες τυγχάνομεν· τέταρτον, ὅπερ μέγιστόν ἐστι, τοὺς μὴ διαφθειρομένους ὑπὸ τῶν εὐπραγιῶν μηδ’ ἐξισταμένους αὑτῶν μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνους γινομένους, ἀλλ’ ἐμμένοντας τῇ τάξει τῶν εὖ φρονούντων. εἶτα ἐπιφέρει τὸν κολοφῶνα τοῦ λόγου· τοὺς δὲ μὴ μόνον πρὸς ἓν τούτων, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἅπαντα ταῦτα τὴν ἕξιν τῆς ψυχῆς εὐάρμοστον ἔχοντας, τούτους φημὶ καὶ φρονίμους εἶναι καὶ τελείους ἄνδρας καὶ πάσας ἔχειν τὰς ἀρετάς. ὁρᾷς πῶς τὸν γνωστικὸν βίον καὶ Ἕλληνες, καίτοι μὴ εἰδότες ὡς ἐπίστασθαι χρή, ἐκθειάζουσι; τίς δ’ ἔστιν ἡ γνῶσις, οὐδὲ ὄναρ ἴσασιν. Εἰ τοίνυν λογικὸν ἡμῖν βρῶμα ἡ γνῶσις εἶναι συμπεφώνηται, μακάριοι τῷ ὄντι κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν οἱ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ὅτι πλησθήσονται τροφῆς ἀιδίου. πάνυ θαυμαστῶς ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς φιλόσοφος Εὐριπίδης τοῖς προειρημένοις ἡμῖν συνῳδὸς διὰ τούτων εὑρίσκεται, πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν ἅμα οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως αἰνισσόμενος· σοὶ τῷ πάντων μεδέοντι χοὴν πέλανόν τε φέρω, Ζεὺς εἴτ’ Ἀίδης ὀνομαζόμενος στέργεις· σὺ δέ μοι θυσίαν ἄπυρον παγκαρπείας δέξαι πλήρη προχυτίαν. ὁλοκάρπωμα γὰρ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἄπυρον θῦμα ὁ Χριστός. καὶ ὅτι τὸν σωτῆρα αὐτὸν οὐκ εἰδὼς λέγει, σαφὲς ποιήσει ἐπάγων· σὺ γὰρ ἔν τε θεοῖς τοῖς οὐρανίδαις σκῆπτρον τὸ Διὸς μεταχειρίζεις χθονίων τ’ Ἀίδῃ μετέχεις ἀρχῆς. ἔπειτα ἄντικρυς λέγει· πέμψον δ’ ἐς φῶς ψυχὰς ἐνέρων τοῖς βουλομένοις ἄθλους προμαθεῖν πόθεν ἔβλαστον, τίς ῥίζα κακῶν, τίνα δεῖ μακάρων ἐκθυσαμένους εὑρεῖν μοχθῶν ἀνάπαυλαν. οὐκ ἀπεικότως ἄρα καὶ τῶν μυστηρίων τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησιν ἄρχει μὲν τὰ καθάρσια, καθάπερ καὶ τοῖς βαρβάροις τὸ λουτρόν.
pass_a_gloss: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the separation of the body and its passions without regret. This is true reverence for the existing God. And it is not without reason that the study of death is called philosophy by Socrates; for he who neither presents sight in his thinking nor clings to any of the other senses, but encounters things with his pure mind, pursues true philosophy. This is also what Pythagoras means by the silence of five years, which he prescribes for his acquaintances, so that, turning away from sensory things, they may contemplate the divine with a pure mind. The greatest of the Greeks, having philosophized in this way, followed Moses. For he commands that the whole burnt offerings, having been flayed, be divided into parts, since the cognitive soul, having become naked of the material skin and having shed the bodily chatter and all the passions, which the empty and false assumptions produce, and having put off the fleshly desires, must be consecrated to the light. But most people, putting on the mortal, like snails and hedgehogs, and being curled up around their own excesses, think such things about the blessed and immortal God as they do about themselves. It has escaped their notice, even if they are near us, that God has given us countless things, of which He Himself is without share, being unborn, without need of nourishment, and equal in growth, and having a good old age and a good death, being immortal and ageless. Therefore, no one should suppose that hands and feet and mouth and eyes and entrances and exits and organs and threats are passions of God, as is said among the Hebrews; rather, it is more proper to allegorize some of these names, which we will clarify as the discussion proceeds. Wisdom is the panacea of all things, as Callimachus writes in his epigrams; another wise man comes from another, both in the past and in the present, as Bacchylides says in his Paeans; for it is not easy to find the gates of unspoken words. Isocrates, in his Panathenaic Oration, asks what kind of people he considers to be well-educated; he proposes and adds: first, those who use things well, which happen every day, and have a good reputation in their times, and are able to think about what is advantageous for the most part; then, those who converse properly and justly with those who approach them, and easily and readily bear the unpleasantness and heaviness of others, and provide themselves as light and moderate as possible to those who are with them; and also those who master their pleasures and are not overly defeated by their misfortunes, but live bravely in them, and are worthy of the nature in which we participate; fourth, and most importantly, those who are not corrupted by their good fortune, nor do they become arrogant, but remain in the order of those who think well. Then he adds the conclusion of his speech: those who have a disposition of soul that is well-suited not just for one of these things, but for all of them, I say are wise and perfect men, and have all the virtues. Do you see how the cognitive life is praised by the Greeks, even though they do not know how to know? What is knowledge, they do not even dream. If, then, it has been agreed that knowledge is our rational food, blessed are those who hunger and thirst for truth, for they will be filled with eternal food. The philosopher Euripides, on the stage, is found to be in harmony with what has been said, not knowing how to praise the Father and the Son at the same time; he says: I bring you a drink-offering and a bowl of mixture, Zeus, whether you are called Hades or something else; you accept a bloodless sacrifice, full of all fruitfulness. For the Christ is a bloodless, whole sacrifice for us. And that he is speaking without knowing the Savior, he will make clear by adding: for you wield the scepter of Zeus among the heavenly gods, and you share the rule of Hades among the earthly ones. Then he says straightforwardly: send the souls of the dead to the light, so that those who wish to learn may know from what source they sprouted, what is the root of evils, what they must seek, having sacrificed, to find rest from their labors. It is not without reason, then, that the purifications are the beginning of the mysteries among the Greeks, just as the bath is among the barbarians.

pass_b_english: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the separation of the body and its passions without regret, and this is true reverence for the living God. It is not without reason that Socrates calls philosophy a study of death; for the person who neither relies on sight in thinking nor is drawn by any of the other senses, but encounters reality with a pure mind, shares in true philosophy. This is also what Pythagoras intends by the five‑year silence that he prescribes for his followers, so that, turning away from sensible things, they may contemplate the divine with a pure mind. The leading Greek thinkers who philosophized in this way were following Moses. For Moses commands that whole burnt offerings be flayed and divided into parts, since the cognitive soul, once it has been stripped of its material covering and has shed bodily chatter and all the passions that empty, false assumptions generate, and has put off fleshly desires, must be consecrated to the light. Most people, however, clothe themselves in mortality like snails, and curl up around their own excesses like hedgehogs; they conceive of the blessed, immortal God in the same way they think of themselves. It has escaped their notice—even if they live close to us—that God has given us countless gifts of which He Himself has no share: being unbegotten, He has no birth; needing nothing, He requires no nourishment; abiding in equality, He knows no growth; being immortal and ageless, He enjoys a good old age and a good death. Therefore no one should suppose that hands, feet, mouth, eyes, entrances, exits, organs, or threats are passions of God, as they are spoken of among the Hebrews; by no means. It is more proper to allegorize some of these names, which we will clarify in due course as our discussion proceeds.

"Wisdom is the panacea for all things," Callimachus writes in his epigrams; "one wise man springs from another, both in the past and in the present," says Bacchylides in his Paeans, for it is not easy to find the gates of unspoken words. Isocrates, in his Panathenaic Oration, asks what kind of people he calls well‑educated, and he answers: first, those who deal well with the circumstances that confront them each day and possess a good reputation in their times, able to aim for the most part at what is advantageous; then, those who always converse properly and justly with those who approach them, and who bear the unpleasantness and heaviness of others easily and readily, while presenting themselves to their companions as light and moderate as possible; also, those who master their pleasures and are not overly defeated by misfortunes, but conduct themselves bravely in them, proving worthy of the nature in which we share; and fourth, which is most important, those who are not corrupted by good fortune, nor become arrogant, but remain in the order of those who think rightly. He then adds the conclusion of his speech: those who possess a disposition of soul well‑suited not to only one of these things but to all of them—I call these people wise, perfect men, and possessors of every virtue. Do you see how the Greeks, even though they do not know how to know, extol the cognitive life? They do not even dream of what knowledge is. If, then, it has been agreed that knowledge is our rational food, blessed are those who hunger and thirst for truth, for they will be filled with eternal food (Matthew 5:6). The philosopher Euripides, on the stage, is found to harmonize with what has been said, not knowing how to indicate the Father and the Son simultaneously: "To you who care for all things I bring a drink‑offering and a mixing bowl, Zeus—whether you are called Hades or by another name—you who accept a bloodless sacrifice, full of all fruitfulness." For Christ is a bloodless, whole sacrifice for us. And that he speaks without knowing the Savior, he will make clear by adding: "For you wield the scepter of Zeus among the heavenly gods, and you share the rule of Hades among the earthly ones." Then he says outright: "Send the souls of the dead to the light, so that those who wish to learn may know from what source they sprang, what is the root of evils, and what they must seek, having sacrificed, to find rest from their labors." It is not without reason, then, that purifications are the beginning of the mysteries among the Greeks, just as the bath is among the barbarians.
